bodies. Here we use computational modeling to predict the magnetic fields that could be sensed
by NASA’s mission to (16) Psyche, a metal-rich body in the asteroid belt. We find that the strength,
shape and orientation of the magnetic field relative to the spin of (16) Psyche could discriminate

1 Introduction
M-class asteroids were classically interpreted as potential fossil cores of larger planetary
bodies because their visible/near-infrared spectra suggested compositional similarities with iron
meteorites (Bell et al., 1989). With an average diameter of 233 km, (16) Psyche is the largest M-
class asteroid and a natural target for exploration (Elkins-Tanton et al., 2020). However, more re-
cent imaging and analyses indicate that (16) Psyche’s density of 4160±640 kg m−3 (Drummond
et al., 2018) is lower than that of iron meteorites, strongly suggesting that while still metal rich,
(16) Psyche has a significant porosity and/or is a metal-silicate mixture. This finding raises fas-
cinating possibilities for the nature and evolution of (16) Psyche. For example, it is possible that
(16) Psyche formed with a very thin mantle, discussed as one possibility for the nature of the Main
Group pallasite meteorite parent body (Tarduno et al., 2012; Nichols et al., 2021). Alternatively,
an impact may have stripped (16) Psyche of most of its mantle, leaving a body with some man-
tle over an intact or disrupted core. These scenarios further raise the question of how magnetome-
ter data obtained during NASA’s current mission (Elkins-Tanton et al., 2020; Weiss et al., 2023)
might help distinguish between alternatives for the nature and history experienced by (16) Psy-
che, a topic we take up anew here.
Following pioneering work on meteorite magnetism, it has been recognized that Solar Sys-
tem bodies can be magnetized by external, internal or intrinsic processes (Banerjee & Hargraves,
1972; Nagata, 1979). External processes include direct magnetization by nebular or solar wind
fields. In addition, impacts are an external process that can magnetize bodies by impact plume-
driven compression of the ambient solar wind field (Hood, 1987) or charge separation in the im-
pact plasma (Crawford, 2020). Internal processes usually invoke a core dynamo, but for a large
planetary body this might be a mantle magma ocean dynamo (e.g. Stixrude et al. (2020)). In-
trinsic processes refer to the characteristic of some FeNi magnetic minerals, particularly those
of iron meteorites, to acquire a remanent magnetization when cooled in a zero magnetic field (Brecher
& Albright, 1977) and/or by interactions between adjacent magnetic minerals (Dunlop & ¨Ozdemir,
1997; O’Brien et al., 2020).
Faced with this plethora of magnetization pathways, here we restrict our consideration to
two cases after nebula dispersal: (i) early solar wind-induced magnetization (WIM) imparted when
the present-day (16) Psyche was formed after the impact disruption of a larger body and (ii) a core

of its overlying mantle, which was brought to relatively high temperatures, exceeding the block-
ing temperature of FeNi magnetic minerals (∼360 to 760°C, Dunlop & ¨Ozdemir (1997)), and
that these minerals acquired a thermoremanent magnetization when cooled in the ambient, ram
pressure- amplified solar wind field of the early Solar System (O’Brien et al., 2020; Anand et al.,
2021). For case (ii) we consider that (16) Psyche could be a largely intact body with an appre-
ciable silicate mantle able to record a core dynamo field, or a small fragment from the mantle of
a disrupted rubble body that was itself magnetized by a dynamo.
Assumptions about the magnetized material are essential because iron meteorites are no-
toriously poor magnetic recorders (Nagata, 1978). Any ancient magnetizations held by huge mul-
tidomain and low coercivity kamacite grains common in iron meteorites could have relaxed in
the billions of years since the early Solar System. In contrast, much smaller single domain FeNi
grains found in a silicate mantle can retain magnetizations on multi-billion-year timescales (Tar-

iron meteorites enhances the possibility that a diagnostic magnetic signature will be recorded.

tionable. We will revisit these magnetization assumptions, as well as the age of magnetization
relative to dispersal of the solar nebular, in our discussion of results.
We carry out magnetohydrodynamic calculations using the adaptive mesh refinement (AMR)
code AstroBEAR (Cunningham et al., 2009; Carroll-Nellenback et al., 2013), to better understand
the magnetization scenarios (i-ii) described above. O’Brien et al. (2020) and Anand et al. (2021)
previously used this code to investigate the magnetizing potential of the early solar wind, shortly
after the clearing of dust and gas of the solar nebula. When encountering a spherical carbona-
ceous chondrite asteroid, the field was found to be amplified to values ∼1 µT for bodies at or-
bital radii equal to or less than those of the present-day asteroid belt. The case considered by O’Brien
et al. (2020) and Anand et al. (2021) addressed the potential to magnetize, on time scales less than
a solar reversal cycle period, a near surface sample represented by a meteorite, and magnetic min-
erals that formed by metasomatic reactions common on early carbonaceous chondrite parent bod-
ies. Hence, this magnetization is a low temperature chemical or crystallization remanent mag-
netization.

the previous work, we use the amplified magnetic field from the simulations as the externally ap-

Psyche over various acquisition time scales to represent the thermoremanent magnetization of
the entire body whose external field might be sensed by a satellite. For comparison, we use a sim-
ilar procedure to predict the remanent field that would arise from internal and external core dy-
namos (case (ii) above).

For impact induced magnetic acquisition, the orbital phase immediately after the collision
determines the angle of the wind to the spin axis, which in turn strongly influences the predicted
field configuration. A higher magnitude quadrupole corresponds to higher asymmetry between
Northern and Southern hemispheres. As such, 𝜃cannot be 0° or 90°, and 𝜑cannot be 90° for any

separations between the spin axis and each of the three coordinate axes, which manifests in the
orientation of the surface remanent magnetization.
If (16) Psyche cooled at its present-day inclination over a few orbital time periods, then an
average of cases P1-8 is needed to predict the observed solar wind induced magnetic field. This
is shown as case PA in Fig. 2(d) and Table 1. Here the toroidal component of the surface dipole
and any hemispherical asymmetry averages out, leaving a sizeable dipole term but no quadrupole.
3.2 Core Dynamo Magnetization
For the case of magnetization by a core dynamo (Fig 2f) we first consider Runcorn’s the-
orem (Runcorn, 1975), which implies that the remanent dipole term of a spherical shell magne-
tized by an internal dipole source vanishes. This happens because the radius of the shell is in-
dependent of the polar or azimuthal angle. (16) Psyche is an elliptical body, but we have found

that for moderately elliptical axi-symmetric shells the dipole term is still quite small. The result
is a relatively weak multipolar field.
In contrast, if we consider (16) Psyche to be a small fragment of a body magnetized by a
larger dipole, possibly representing a silicate mantle component with magnetic minerals that could
preserve an ancient field, the resultant field is itself a dipole (Fig. 2e). Since it is statistically un-
likely for the spin axis of the fragmented asteroid be aligned with the parent body’s core dynamo
dipole field axis, the global field would generically look like a tilted dipole. The resulting global
magnetic field is potentially the strongest of all cases explicitly modeled here. The surface re-
manent magnetization is not shown for this case as the entire volume is the magnetized fragment
that composes the asteroid.
4 Discussion: Influence of Acquisition Time, Asteroid Geometry, and Present Solar Wind
The strength of any remanent field potentially exhibited by (16) Psyche will depend on the
asteroid’s material properties, as well as the thermal and magnetic history of the surface layers
over the acquisition time. A threshold value of Mp = 2 × 1014A m−2 has been estimated for
any field detection by the Psyche mission magnetometer Weiss et al. (2023) by having a stand-
off distance outside the asteroid, which is assumed to be spherical. This may need favorable so-
lar illumination conditions (NASA/JPL-Caltech, 2023), ideally an equinox, given (16) Psyche
is triaxial and tilted at 98°. Here, we assume that the magnetic susceptibility is the same for both
the core dynamo and the solar wind induced magnetization cases.
The solar wind induced magnetization acquisition time in our case (i) is set by the post-
collisional cooling rate. The fastest scenario would be instantaneous cooling following a slow
(∼2 km/s) collision with another asteroid (Bland et al., 2014; Muxworthy et al., 2017). How-
ever, for asteroids rich in iron bearing minerals, the thermal conductivity is much higher (Soini
et al., 2020) and is an efficient mechanism for cooling over a few hours to a few years depend-
ing on the depth of the impacted layers. Here, we largely follow this fast acquisition time scenario.
For an acquisition time less than an orbit time, the asteroid’s orbital position affects the observed
field (see results from 8 different simulations corresponding to different locations in (16) Psy-
che’s orbit shown in Table 1). Table 1 shows that the dipole moment (mz) depends most strongly
on the axial tilt (𝜃), with only a slight dependence on the orbital phase (𝜑). This value of 𝜃could
have changed over time due to collisions, internal processes, tidal forces, secular perturbations,
or thermal (such as Yarkovsky) effects. The last 3 effects are extremely slow. For the dynamo case,
if (16) Psyche’s parent body cooled from the crust toward the core (Scheinberg et al., 2016), the
timescale for the relevant magnetized components could be thousands to millions of years. We
assume the dynamo is relatively steady over the acquisition timescale.
We model the asteroid as a biaxial ellipsoid with spin axis along the shorter axis. This means
an azimuthal symmetry such that spin averaging cancels 𝑚> 0 modes exactly is not expected
for a real asteroid. However, the 𝑚= 0 modes of the magnetic scalar potential in equation 2 do
not depend on the averaging procedure. As such, we expect triaxial and even non-uniform aster-
oids to have the same 𝑚= 0 mode global field structure at Orbit C distances (190 km altitude).
Our model does not completely capture the weak multipolar field at large distances or the near
surface field structure, which will be undetectable at the orbital radii typical of the Psyche space-
craft.
The present day solar wind will interact with the remanent field and create a magnetopause
outside (16) Psyche if Mp > 2×1014A m−2. Fatemi & Poppe (2018) simulated the interaction
of present day solar wind for both magnetized and unmagnetized (16) Psyche using a hybrid code
that tracks ions separately from fluid electrons. We can use their simulations to analytically as-
sess the implications of the effect of the present day solar wind on our results. The standoff dis-
tance of the magnetopause for taking the best case net dipole moment, Mp = 2.5 × 1014A m2
from the P-cases in Table 1, and present day solar wind values of velocity, 𝑣= 400 km s−1, and
density, 𝜌= 1 H+cm−3, is

In order for the closest approach of Psyche (75 km above the surface or ∼213 km from
the center) to be inside the magnetopause, such that a field can be detected and partially charac-
terized irrespective of illumination conditions, a dipole moment Mp > 1.25 × 1015A m2 is re-

need 2x stronger dynamo. For the WIM cases, the magnetic field observable by the orbiter will
scale linearly with magnetization depth as per equation (1). Fully mapping the field irrespective
of illumination at Orbit C will need Mp > 2.6 × 1015A m2.
As the internal structure of (16) Psyche is still unknown, we have also considered the pos-
sibility that it may have differentiated with a core that is orders of magnitude more conductive
than the surrounding regions, but without an active dynamo. Using the framework of a previous
study (Anand et al., 2021), we varied the size of the core to identify the core size that maximizes
the solar wind induced magnetic field. We find that when the core is 75% the radius of the body,
the crust field increased by only about ∼20% compared to a body having no core, so the influ-
ence on the solar WIM is not significant (see Supplementary Material).

5 Conclusions and Future Directions
We computed predictions for the axisymmetric, 𝑚= 0, mode of dipole and quadrupole
terms of the global magnetic field around (16) Psyche-like asteroids for solar WIM and core dy-
namo origins, and for different cooling timescales and asteroid spin orientations. We find that
whether (16) Psyche acquired magnetization as a fragment of a larger parent body with an inter-
nal dynamo, versus external WIM can be determined by a combination of strength and topology
of the field as long as sufficient data from both hemispheres is available. In particular, the ratio
of the dipole to the quadrupole term is significantly smaller for the WIM and the presence of higher
order modes and multipoles would further suggest external WIM. The parent body dynamo case
also has a factor ∼4 times stronger remanent field as potentially the entire volume of the aster-
oid is magnetized. A strong global dipole field substantially tilted to the asteroid’s spin axis would
suggest magnetization as part of a larger parent body. If instead of a coherent global field, the or-
biter measures scattered pockets of local field, (i) for the parent dynamo case this could imply
re-accretion of randomly oriented fragments to the main asteroid body or (ii) for the WIM case,
magnetized of multiple smaller regions of the crust from different impacts. A complete absence
of magnetic field would place an upper bound on the depth of the crust that can be magnetized
by WIM, including the solar nebula wind.
There is currently no precise estimate of the epoch when (16) Psyche formed, as no me-
teorite samples are believed to have originated from the same parent body. The proto-solar tur-
bulent nebular disk might not have cleared before (16) Psyche cooled and could have magnetized
the asteroid via WIM from the nebular field. Asteroid cooling in the presence of the solar neb-
ula could take many eddy crossing timescales in which case the interaction with many individ-
ual eddies with differently aligned magnetic fields would require averag. Even conservatively ac-
counting for field reversals during a cooling timescale lasting 100s of orbits, the conversion of
ram pressure to magnetic energy would seemingly produce larger magnetic field strengths than
either solar WIM or remanent magnetization from the core dynamo of a larger parent body. The
field would then be more highly multipolar and structurally distinct from solar WIM or dynamo
sources. However, for large bodies, the bow shock reduces the effective ram pressure on the as-
teroid (Mai et al., 2018) and would weaken this nebular magnetic field amplification. More work
is needed on this nebular WIM for comparison with the two other field origin sources that we fo-
cused on.
Finally, if the surface of (16) Psyche were directly magnetized by an impact which heated
and cooled its outer layers rapidly compared to the rotation/tumbling rate of the asteroid, the outer
layer would directly record the amplified magnetic field from the ambient wind. This would re-
sult in a large but highly localized field at the impact site or its antipode (Crawford, 2020) and
thereby induce very high order multipolar modes. High order modes could also arise if the crustal
magnetic mineral composition is inhomogeneous, but this may be unlikely if (16) Psyche formed
as a small fragment from the crust of a larger body. In that case, a highly asymmetric measured
field would suggest external WIM, whereas a symmetric field would suggest a dynamo in the pro-
genitor body.
